subtopic: CUDA Event vs CPU Timer: single-kernel timing
learningObjective: Choose between CUDA events and CPU timers when timing a single small CUDA kernel; understand the precision and semantic implications.
stem: You want to time a single small CUDA kernel (expected duration ~30 µs) that runs on a non-default stream in the middle of a larger workload. Which measurement approach is most accurate, and why?
profileData:
Setup:
  - Kernel duration expected ~30 µs
  - Runs on user stream `s1`, while stream `s2` runs concurrent work
  - Wall-clock question: time _only_ this one kernel, not the concurrent work

Candidate approaches:
  (i)   time.perf_counter() around a single non-synced launch
  (ii)  time.perf_counter() around launch + torch.cuda.synchronize() (device-wide)
  (iii) cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), event.record(s1) before and after kernel, elapsed_time after event.synchronize()
  (iv)  time.perf_counter() around launch + s1.synchronize()

options.text: Approach (i) is best because it eliminates any synchronization overhead; the reported time is exactly the wall-clock cost of the launch and it also captures the GPU-side execution because CUDA launches block the host until completion when the kernel is small enough (<100 µs).

Approach (ii) is best because a device-wide synchronize also flushes work on `s2` before recording the end time, which gives the most accurate measurement of _only_ the kernel of interest by ensuring the entire GPU is idle at the endpoints.

Approach (iii) is best: CUDA events recorded on `s1` around the kernel isolate its execution on that stream, are timed by the GPU with ~0.5 µs resolution, and are unaffected by concurrent work on `s2`. Approaches using device-wide synchronize would also charge concurrent work on other streams.

Approach (iv) is best because a stream-scoped synchronize combined with a CPU timer captures the full CPU dispatch cost plus GPU execution; CUDA events cannot record a stream because `cudaEventRecord` only accepts the default stream in single-context CUDA programs.

explanation: CUDA events with `enable_timing=True` are recorded onto the target stream and time GPU-side execution with sub-microsecond resolution. They isolate `s1`'s work and are not perturbed by concurrent work on `s2`. A device-wide synchronize (ii) forces all streams to drain and, combined with a CPU timer, over-charges the measurement with `s2`'s work. Approach (i) is completely wrong (CUDA launches are async). Approach (iv) is misleading: `s1.synchronize()` waits for `s1` only, but the CPU timer also captures dispatch and driver-visible latency, and CUDA events can be recorded on any stream (D's premise is false).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: kernel launches are always asynchronous; a CPU timer around a launch measures dispatch, not execution.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: device-wide synchronize charges `s2`'s concurrent work into the measurement, over-reporting the target kernel's cost.
optionExplanations.C: Correct: stream-scoped CUDA events give per-stream isolation and high timing resolution.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: CUDA events can be recorded on any stream, not only the default stream.

assumptions: Modern CUDA runtime; `cudaEventRecord` supports non-default streams.
Concurrent work on `s2` may overlap in wall clock but is not the measurement target.
nonImplications: Does not imply CUDA events are always the right tool; for coarse workflow-level timing, CPU timers with synchronize are fine.
Does not imply event timing has zero overhead; event record itself adds a few hundred nanoseconds of driver work.

distractorRationales.D: False claim about event stream restrictions.

performanceClaim.scope: Single small CUDA kernel timing with concurrent streams
